name: Introduction to AI and Digital Confidence
objectives: Given a list of five tasks, identify which everyday tasks an AI assistant can help with and which need a person or an official source, getting at least 4 of 5 right
Using a phone or a library computer, open a free AI assistant from its official app or website, send a first message and sign out when you finish, without help
Given a real task from your own life, write a prompt that says what you need, your situation and how you want the answer, so the first answer is useful
Given an AI answer that is not quite right, ask follow-up requests, one at a time, to change it, until it is short, clear and fits your need in no more than three tries
Given an AI answer that includes a fact such as a phone number, address or rule, check the fact on an official website (.gov or the organization's own site), before you use it
When you write a prompt or get an urgent message, keep private information out and spot the warning signs of a scam, sharing no private numbers, passwords or codes

lessons.title: Lesson 1: What an AI assistant is, and what it is not
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 4 minutes
Goal: Explain in your own words what an AI assistant can and cannot do.
This lesson builds toward: Given a list of five tasks, you will identify which everyday tasks an AI assistant can help with and which need a person or an official source, getting at least 4 of 5 right.
An AI assistant is a computer program you can type or talk to in everyday words. You ask a question, and it writes an answer. Well-known free ones include ChatGPT, Microsoft Copilot and Google Gemini.
It learned from a huge amount of writing, so it is good at explaining things, writing drafts, making lists and plans, and putting hard words into simple words.
It is not a person, a lawyer, a doctor or a government office. It does not know you, and it can be wrong, even when it sounds sure. You stay in charge: you decide what to ask, and you decide what to believe.
Words to know:
- AI: short for artificial intelligence: computer programs that do tasks that usually need a person, like writing or answering questions.
- AI assistant: an AI program you chat with by typing or talking.
Try it now: Write down three things in your own life an AI assistant could help with this week, for example a grocery list, a message to a family member, or explaining a letter you got.
You can now say what an AI assistant is, name three things it can help with, and say why you still check what it tells you.

check.q: Which task can an AI assistant help with?
options: Writing a grocery list from the meals you plan
Signing a legal form for you
Paying your bills from your bank
Going to your appointment for you
check.why: An AI assistant can write and explain things; it cannot sign, pay or show up for you.

check.q: An AI assistant tells you a court date. What is true?
options: It is always right because it is a computer
It may be wrong, so you check with the court
Only the AI can change the date
You do not need to write it down
check.why: AI can sound sure and still be wrong; dates and rules come from the official office.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Opening a free AI assistant on a phone or library computer
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Open a free AI assistant and find the box where you type.
This lesson builds toward: Using a phone or a library computer, you will open a free AI assistant from its official app or website, send a first message and sign out when you finish, without help.
You can use an AI assistant on a smartphone or on any computer with internet, such as one at a public library or a job center.
On a phone: open the app store (Google Play on Android, the App Store on iPhone), search for the assistant's name, and install the app made by the real company (OpenAI for ChatGPT, Microsoft for Copilot, Google for Gemini). Only install from the official app store.
On a computer: open the web browser and type the address: chatgpt.com, copilot.microsoft.com or gemini.google.com. Some let you chat without an account; some ask you to sign in.
On a shared or library computer, do not let the browser save your password, and sign out and close the browser when you finish.
Step by step:
- Choose a phone or a computer with internet.
- Phone: install the official app from the app store. Computer: type the web address in the browser.
- Look for the message box near the bottom of the screen. It often says "Ask anything" or "Message".
- On a shared computer: sign out and close the browser when you are done.
Words to know:
- Web browser: the program you use to visit websites, like Chrome, Edge or Safari.
- App store: the official place on a phone to get apps safely.
Try it now: Open one free AI assistant on a phone or computer. Find the message box and type: Hello, I am learning to use AI. Read what it says back.
You can now open a free AI assistant on a phone or a computer, find where to type, and leave a shared computer safely.

check.q: You want an AI app on your phone. Where do you get it?
options: A link in a text from a stranger
Any website with a free download button
The official app store, from the real company
A copy a friend sends you in a message
check.why: The official app store and the real company's name keep fake apps off your phone.

check.q: You are done using AI on a library computer. What do you do first?
options: Leave it open for the next person
Turn off the screen only
Write your password on a note
Sign out and close the browser
check.why: Signing out and closing the browser keeps the next person out of your chats and accounts.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Asking a clear question
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Write a clear request that gets a useful answer the first time.
This lesson builds toward: Given a real task from your own life, you will write a prompt that says what you need, your situation and how you want the answer, so the first answer is useful.
What you type to an AI assistant is called a prompt. A clear prompt gets a better answer.
A good prompt has three parts: what you need, a little about your situation (without private details), and how you want the answer. For example: "I start a new warehouse job Monday at 7 am. Make me a simple checklist for the night before. Use short sentences."
A weak prompt is too short, like "job tips". The assistant has to guess what you mean, so the answer is general.
Step by step:
- Say what you need.
- Add a little about your situation, with no private details.
- Say how you want the answer: short, simple words, steps, a list or a table.
Words to know:
- Prompt: what you type or say to an AI assistant to ask for something.
Try it now: Pick one real task from your list in Lesson 1. Write a prompt with all three parts, send it, and read the answer.
You can now write a prompt with what you need, your situation and how you want the answer.

check.q: Which prompt has all three parts: what you need, your situation and how you want the answer?
options: "Help me."
"I have a warehouse job interview Tuesday. Give me 5 common questions in a short list."
"Write a list."
"Interview."
check.why: It says what you need (questions), your situation (warehouse interview Tuesday) and the format (a short list of 5).

check.q: Your prompt says what you need and your situation. What is missing?
options: How you want the answer, like short steps or a list
Your full name and date of birth
A thank-you note
Nothing; it is complete
check.why: Saying how you want the answer (short, simple, steps, a list) is the third part of a clear prompt.

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Making an answer better
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 4 minutes
Goal: Ask follow-up questions to improve an answer.
This lesson builds toward: Given an AI answer that is not quite right, you will ask follow-up requests, one at a time, to change it, until it is short, clear and fits your need in no more than three tries.
You do not have to accept the first answer. An AI assistant remembers what you said earlier in the same chat, so you can ask it to change its answer.
Useful follow-ups: "Make it shorter." "Use simpler words." "Explain step 2 more." "Give me an example." "Put it in a list." "Make it sound more polite."
If the chat goes off track, start a new chat and write a clearer prompt.
Step by step:
- Read the first answer.
- Decide what you want changed.
- Ask for that one change.
- Repeat until the answer works for you.
Words to know:
- Follow-up: a second question that builds on the answer you got.
Try it now: Take the answer from Lesson 3. Ask for two changes, one at a time, such as "make it shorter" and then "use simpler words". Compare the first and last answers.
You can now improve an AI answer by asking clear follow-up questions.

check.q: The answer uses words that are hard to read. What do you send next?
options: "Wrong. Try again."
Nothing; close the app
"Make it longer."
"Use simpler words."
check.why: A clear follow-up that says the change you want fixes the answer without starting over.

check.q: Why ask for changes one at a time?
options: The AI can only read one word at a time
You can see what each change did
It costs less money
The AI gets upset with long requests
check.why: One change at a time shows you which request made the answer better.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Checking the answer before you trust it
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Check an AI answer against a trusted source.
This lesson builds toward: Given an AI answer that includes a fact such as a phone number, address or rule, you will check the fact on an official website (.gov or the organization's own site), before you use it.
AI assistants sometimes make things up, such as a wrong phone number, an office that does not exist, an old rule or a wrong date. This is sometimes called a hallucination.
Always check anything about money, the law, your health, government benefits, dates, addresses and phone numbers. Check with the official source: a government website (the address usually ends in .gov), the office itself, or a person you trust such as a case manager, reentry counselor or librarian.
A good habit: ask the assistant "Where can I check this?" and then go to that official page yourself, instead of trusting a link without looking.
Step by step:
- Find the facts in the answer: numbers, dates, names, rules.
- Look them up on the official site (often ending in .gov) or call the office.
- If they do not match, trust the official source.
- For big decisions, also ask a person you trust.
Words to know:
- Hallucination: when an AI writes something that sounds true but is made up.
- .gov: the ending of official United States government website addresses.
Try it now: Ask an AI assistant for the phone number or website of a real office near you (for example your state's motor vehicle office). Then find the office's official website yourself and see if the answer matches.
You can now spot facts that need checking and check them with an official source.

check.q: The AI gives you a phone number for the motor vehicle office. What do you do?
options: Find the number on the office's official website and compare
Call it right away
Share it online
Ask the AI if it is sure
check.why: Only the official website can confirm the number; the AI can make up numbers that look real.

check.q: Which web address is most likely an official US government website?
options: dmv-help-now.com
freegovforms.net
dmv.ca.gov
govservices.info
check.why: Official US government websites usually end in .gov.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Keeping your private information safe
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Use AI without sharing private information, and spot AI-powered scams.
This lesson builds toward: When you write a prompt or get an urgent message, you will keep private information out and spot the warning signs of a scam, sharing no private numbers, passwords or codes.
Do not type private information into an AI assistant: your Social Security number, ID numbers, case or inmate numbers, passwords, bank or card numbers, or full home address. You can get the help you need without them. Write "[my number]" instead.
Scammers use AI too. They can write messages that look real and even copy a family member's voice on a phone call. Be careful with any message that rushes you, asks for money or gift cards, or asks for a code that was sent to your phone.
If something feels wrong, stop. Hang up, and call the person or office back using a number you already know is real.
Step by step:
- Before you send a prompt, read it for private information and take it out.
- Use a placeholder like "[my number]".
- Treat rushed messages, money requests and code requests as warning signs.
- Call back using a number you know is real.
Words to know:
- Private information: details that could let someone pretend to be you or take your money.
- Scam: a trick to steal money or information.
Try it now: Final task: use an AI assistant to write a short, polite message asking a business whether it is hiring. Ask for one change to make it better, check it has no private information, and read it out loud.
You can now use an AI assistant for a real task while keeping your private information safe, and spot the signs of a scam.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Clear request The prompt is vague, for example "write a message". The prompt says what you need, your situation and how you want the answer. It also names the business and the job, and the first answer is close to ready. Made it better Used the first answer as it was. Asked for one change and the message got better. Asked for two or more changes, one at a time, and can say what each one fixed. Private information kept out The prompt or message has a private number, password, address or date of birth. No private information in the prompt or the message. Used a placeholder like [my phone number] and filled it in only in the message they send themselves. Facts checked A business name, address or hours were copied from the AI without checking. Any fact about the business was checked on its own website or an official listing. Can say where they checked it. Sounds like you The message uses words the learner would not say or does not understand. Read out loud, it is polite, short and in the learner's own words. The learner changed some words themselves to sound more like them. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part and try again.

check.q: A job form asks for your Social Security number and you want AI help with it. What do you type?
options: Your real number so the AI can check it
Your number with one digit changed
Your bank card number instead
A placeholder like [my number]
check.why: A placeholder lets the AI help with the wording while your real number stays private.

check.q: A text says your benefits stop today unless you send the code you were just sent. What is this?
options: A scam; never share the code
A normal message from your office
A test you must pass
A reminder to update your phone
check.why: Rushing you and asking for a code are warning signs of a scam; real offices do not ask for these codes.
